title: CSC3710 2026-11-12: Regular Expression to NFA-λ, λ-Closure, Input Transition Function

questions.q: Because NFA-λs allow nondeterminism and λ-transitions, they can accept some languages that no DFA accepts.
questions.explain: DFAs, NFAs and NFA-λs all accept exactly the regular languages. Nondeterminism and λ-moves feel more powerful, but they don't add any languages to the class.

questions.q: Which class of languages do NFA-λs accept?
choices: A strict superset of the regular languages
A strict subset of the regular languages
questions.explain: NFA-λs accept exactly the regular languages, just like DFAs, NFAs and regular grammars.

questions.q: Which sets are in the basis of the recursive definition of regular sets over an alphabet Σ?
questions.explain: The basis is ∅, {λ}, and {a} for each symbol a. Sets like Σ* and {ab} are regular, but they come from the recursive step, not the basis.

questions.q: Which operations appear in the recursive step of the definition of regular sets?
questions.explain: If X and Y are regular, then X ∪ Y, XY and X* are regular. The construction of NFA-λs has one rule for each of these three operations.

questions.q: To show that the set described by (a ∪ b)*ba is regular, {ba} must be built before {a, b}, or the argument fails.
questions.explain: Any valid build-up works. {ba} and {a, b}* are independent pieces, so either one can be built first. Only the final concatenation {a, b}*{ba} has to come last.

questions.q: The regex-to-NFA-λ construction mirrors the recursive definition of regular sets: one machine for each basis set, plus a way to build a machine for each operation from the machines of its parts. So every regular language has an NFA-λ.
questions.explain: Every regular set is produced by the recursive definition, and each step of that definition has a matching machine construction.

questions.q: The construction keeps every machine in a standard form (given by a lemma). What is that form?
choices: Exactly one start state with no arrows into it and exactly one final state with no arrows out of it
Exactly one start state with no arrows out of it and exactly one final state with no arrows into it
No λ-transitions, and every state has exactly one transition for each symbol
Exactly one start state, and every state except the start state is final
questions.explain: Nothing points into the start and nothing leaves the final, so the machine dangles between two handles that can be wired to other machines without creating unintended paths.

questions.q: Which basis machine accepts ∅?
choices: A start state and a final state with no transitions
A start state and a final state joined by a λ-transition
A single state that is both start and final
A start state and a final state joined by an a-transition
questions.explain: With no transitions the final state can't be reached, so nothing is accepted. The λ-joined machine accepts {λ}, and the a-joined machine accepts {a}.

questions.q: Building a machine for L(M1) ∪ L(M2) adds how many states and λ-transitions?
questions.explain: Union adds a new start and a new final state, plus λ-transitions from the new start to both old starts and from both old finals to the new final.

questions.q: M1 has start s1 and final f1, and M2 has start s2 and final f2. For the union, a new start s and a new final f are added. Which λ-transitions are added?
questions.explain: Union: λ from s to each old start, and λ from each old final to f. f1 → s2 belongs to concatenation, and s → f belongs to Kleene star.

questions.q: To build a machine for L(M1)L(M2), where M1 has start s1 and final f1 and M2 has start s2 and final f2, which single λ-transition is added?
questions.explain: Concatenation puts M1 on the left and M2 on the right and joins them with one λ-transition from M1's final to M2's start.

questions.q: After building the concatenation L(M1)L(M2) (M1: start s1, final f1; M2: start s2, final f2), which statements are true?
choices: f1 is no longer a final state
s2 is no longer a start state
f2 is the only final state
s1 is no longer a start state
A new start state is added
questions.explain: Concatenation adds no states. s1 stays the start, f2 becomes the only final, f1 loses its final status, and s2 loses its start status.

questions.q: In the concatenation construction, it doesn't matter which machine goes on the left and which goes on the right.
questions.explain: Order matters. For L(M1)L(M2), M1's machine goes on the left, because XY and YX are generally different languages.

questions.q: For the Kleene star L(M1)*, a new start and a new final state are added. Which four λ-transitions are added?
questions.explain: Star: new start → new final (accepts λ), old final → old start (repeat), new start → old start (enter M1), old final → new final (exit). The old final loses its final status.

questions.q: In the Kleene star construction, what is the λ-transition from the new start state to the new final state for?
choices: It lets the machine accept λ (zero repetitions)
It lets the machine repeat M1's language
It connects the star machine to the next piece
It keeps the new final state free of outgoing arrows
questions.explain: X* always contains λ. The direct λ from the new start to the new final accepts zero repetitions. Repeating comes from the old final → old start transition.

questions.q: In the Kleene star construction, the λ-transition from the old final state back to the old start state is what lets M1's language be repeated.
questions.explain: After one pass through M1, the λ from the old final back to the old start lets the machine go around again.

questions.q: Which operation in the construction adds no new states?
questions.explain: Concatenation adds only one λ-transition (f1 → s2). Union and star each add 2 states and 4 λ-transitions.

questions.q: A machine for a*b that is NOT in standard form: start q0 has an a-loop, q0 –b→ q1, and q1 is final. A shortcut for star makes q0 final and adds a λ from q1 to q0. Which string does the result wrongly accept as part of (a*b)*?
questions.explain: Every nonempty string in (a*b)* ends in b. With q0 final, reading a loops on q0 and stops in a final state, so a is accepted. The theorem's new states and standard-form machines prevent paths like this.

questions.q: Following the construction exactly (no simplifying), how many states does the NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba have?
questions.explain: 4 basis machines × 2 states = 8, plus 2 for the union and 2 for the star, gives 12. Concatenations add no states.

questions.q: Following the construction exactly, how many λ-transitions does the NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba have?
questions.explain: Union 4 + star 4 + concatenation for ba 1 + final concatenation 1 = 10. There are also 4 symbol transitions.

questions.q: Without drawing it, how many states does the construction produce for (ab)* ∪ a?
questions.explain: Basis machines for a, b, a give 6 states. ab adds 0, (ab)* adds 2, and the union with a adds 2. Total 10 (with 9 λ-transitions).

questions.q: Without drawing it, how many states does the construction produce for a*b*?
questions.explain: Each basis machine has 2 states and each star adds 2, so a* and b* have 4 states each. The concatenation adds none. Total 8.

questions.q: Without drawing it, how many λ-transitions does the construction produce for (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)?
questions.explain: Each union adds 4 λ-transitions (8 total), and the concatenation adds 1. Total 9.

questions.q: Following the construction exactly, how many λ-transitions does the NFA-λ for a*b have?
questions.explain: The star on a adds 4 λ-transitions and the concatenation with b adds 1. Total 5 (and 6 states).

questions.q: When applying the construction, you should delete λ-transitions that are obviously unnecessary, such as the one inside the machine for ba, to keep the machine correct.
questions.explain: Don't simplify. The theorem is generic and works on any machines, and simplifying by hand is a common source of errors. The goal here is not minimization.

questions.q: Every concatenation in the construction gets its own λ-transition, even when it joins two single-symbol machines like the ones for b and a.
questions.explain: Concatenation always adds one λ from the left machine's final to the right machine's start. Skipping it is an error.

questions.q: Why should you follow the construction exactly instead of simplifying while you build?
choices: The theorem is generic, and shortcuts often break the machine
Removing a λ-transition always changes the start state
A DFA can only be built from an unsimplified NFA-λ
Simplified machines can never accept the empty string
questions.explain: The construction is guaranteed correct for any machines in standard form. Ad hoc shortcuts can add or remove accepted strings.

questions.q: When building the NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba from its parts, which operation is applied last?
choices: Concatenate the (a ∪ b)* machine with the ba machine
Apply Kleene star to the a ∪ b machine
Take the union of the a machine and the b machine
Concatenate the b machine with the a machine
questions.explain: The outermost operation is the concatenation of (a ∪ b)* with ba, so that step comes last. The other steps build its parts.

questions.q: In the NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba, the union machine for a ∪ b has start 2 and final 7. The star step adds a new start 1 and a new final 8. Which rule produced the λ-transition 1 → 8?
choices: Kleene star: new start to new final
Kleene star: old final to new final
Union: new start to old start
Concatenation of the star machine with ba
questions.explain: 1 is the star's new start and 8 is its new final. The λ from 1 to 8 lets the star accept λ.

questions.q: In the NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba, the union machine for a ∪ b has start 2 and final 7, and the star step wraps it with new states 1 and 8. The λ-transition 7 → 2 is the star's old-final-to-old-start transition.
questions.explain: 7 is the old final and 2 is the old start of the machine being starred, so 7 → 2 is the repeat transition.

questions.q: λ-closure(q) can be the empty set.
questions.explain: By the basis of the definition, q ∈ λ-closure(q), so it is never empty.

questions.q: What is λ-closure(q)?
choices: States reachable from q by zero or more λ-moves, including q
States reachable from q by exactly one λ-transition
States reachable from q by reading one input symbol
States that have a λ-transition pointing into q
questions.explain: λ-closure(q) is q plus every state reachable for free (without reading input) through any chain of λ-transitions.

questions.q: If q –λ→ p and p –λ→ r, then r ∈ λ-closure(q).
questions.explain: The recursive step follows chains: p is in the closure, and r is one λ-step from p, so r is in the closure too.

questions.q: If no λ-transitions leave state q, then λ-closure(q) = {q}.
questions.explain: Nothing is reachable for free, so only q itself (from the basis) is in its closure.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has states q0, q1, q2, and its only λ-transition is q2 → q1. What is λ-closure(q2)?
questions.explain: q2 is in its own closure (basis), and q1 is reachable by the λ-transition.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has states q0–q3 and transitions q0 –λ→ q1, q0 –a→ q1, q0 –b→ q2, q1 –b→ q1, q1 –b→ q3, q2 –λ→ q3, q3 –a→ q0, q3 –b→ q2. What is λ-closure(q2)?
questions.explain: q3 is reachable by λ, and q2 itself belongs by the basis. Leaving out the state itself is a common mistake.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is λ-closure(1)?
questions.explain: From 1: λ to 2 and 8, from 2 to 3 and 5, from 8 to 9. Include 1 itself. 10 needs a b-step, so it isn't free.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is λ-closure(4)?
questions.explain: 4 → 7, then 7 → 8 → 9 and 7 → 2 → 3, 5. Plus 4 itself. Forgetting 7 → 2 gives the incomplete {4, 7, 8, 9}.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. Which of these states are in λ-closure(6)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(6) = {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}. 1 has no λ-transitions pointing into it, and 10 is only reachable by reading b.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is λ-closure(7)?
questions.explain: 7 → 2 → 3, 5 and 7 → 8 → 9, plus 7 itself. 4 needs an a-step from 3, so it isn't included.

questions.q: How is t(q, a) computed?
choices: λ-closure of q, then one a-step, then λ-closure of each landing state
One a-step from q, then the λ-closure of q itself
λ-closure of q, then any number of a-steps, then λ-closure
λ-closure of q, then one a-step, with no closure afterward
questions.explain: t(q, a) = λ*, then exactly one a, then λ*: the union of λ-closure(δ(qj, a)) over every qj in λ-closure(q).

questions.q: Unlike λ-closure(q), t(q, a) can be the empty set.
questions.explain: If no state in λ-closure(q) has an a-step, then t(q, a) = ∅. For example, t(3, b) = ∅ in the machine for (a ∪ b)*ba.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has states q0–q3 and transitions q0 –λ→ q1, q0 –a→ q1, q0 –b→ q2, q1 –b→ q1, q1 –b→ q3, q2 –λ→ q3, q3 –a→ q0, q3 –b→ q2. What is t(q2, a)?
questions.explain: q2 has no a-step, but λ-closure(q2) = {q2, q3}, and q3 –a→ q0. λ-closure(q0) = {q0, q1}. Always start from the whole closure, not just q.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has states q0–q3 and transitions q0 –λ→ q1, q0 –a→ q1, q0 –b→ q2, q1 –b→ q1, q1 –b→ q3, q2 –λ→ q3, q3 –a→ q0, q3 –b→ q2. What is t(q0, b)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(q0) = {q0, q1}. q0 –b→ q2 gives {q2, q3}. q1 –b→ q1 and q1 –b→ q3 give {q1} and {q3}. The union is {q1, q2, q3}.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has states q0–q3 and transitions q0 –λ→ q1, q0 –a→ q1, q0 –b→ q2, q1 –b→ q1, q1 –b→ q3, q2 –λ→ q3, q3 –a→ q0, q3 –b→ q2. t(q3, a) = {q0, q1}. Why is q1 in it?
choices: One a-step lands on q0, and the λ-move q0 → q1 adds q1
The a is read twice: q3 to q0, then q0 to q1
q1 is in λ-closure(q3), so it is always included
q1 can be reached from q3 by reading b and then a
questions.explain: t allows exactly one symbol step. q3 –a→ q0, and the closure after landing adds q1 through λ. It is not a second a-step.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is t(1, b)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(1) = {1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9}. The b-steps are 5 → 6 and 9 → 10. λ-closure(6) ∪ λ-closure(10) = {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} ∪ {10, 11}. {6, 10} forgets the closure after landing.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is t(9, b)?
questions.explain: 9 –b→ 10, and λ-closure(10) = {10, 11}. Reaching 12 would also need 11 –a→ 12, a second symbol step.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is t(3, b)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(3) = {3}, and 3 has no b-step, so there is nowhere to land.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is t(2, a)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(2) = {2, 3, 5}. Only 3 has an a-step (to 4), and λ-closure(4) = {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}.

questions.q: The NFA-λ for (a ∪ b)*ba has states 1–12 (start 1, final 12), λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5, 4→7, 6→7, 7→2, 7→8, 8→9, 10→11, and symbol transitions 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6, 9 –b→ 10, 11 –a→ 12. What is t(10, a)?
questions.explain: 10 has no a-step, but λ-closure(10) = {10, 11}, and 11 –a→ 12. λ-closure(12) = {12}.

questions.q: While computing t(1, b), you use the step 5 –b→ 6. What goes into the result from this step?
questions.explain: Take the λ-closure of the state you land on (6), not the state you stepped from, and not just the landed state by itself.

questions.q: In the machine for (a ∪ b)*ba, once b is used on 5 –b→ 6 while computing t(1, b), it is used up, so the path 1 ⇝ 8 ⇝ 9 –b→ 10 can't also add to t(1, b).
questions.explain: Different paths are separate scenarios, and each one uses b exactly once. t(1, b) is the union of all of them, so both λ-closure(6) and λ-closure(10) are included.
